reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: Key points: a three-person table needs no structure, each added structure relieved a limit but inserted someone new, and the later failures are the price of those additions

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The same small request ships in a day at a three-person table and takes a month in an organization of a thousand

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Eight structures separate the table from the thousand, each added for a real shortage, each adding a wait, almost none removed / This account is a deliberate simplification of one generic organization, not a history, with rough sizes and sourced dates

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Roadmap: nine steps, each told in the same four parts and closed with the same question about who decides, knows, checks and waits

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three People at One Table: Nothing to Wait For ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The simplest organization: three people hear a request, discuss it, build it and ship it the same day

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three People at One Table: Nothing to Wait For ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: At the table none of the three scarce things, attention, judgment and verification, is in short supply

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three People at One Table: Nothing to Wait For ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Even at the table one person's week away already separates who decided, who knew and who checked

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three People at One Table: Nothing to Wait For ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The table depends on three conditions, and every later step starts where growth breaks one of them

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three People at One Table: Nothing to Wait For ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Recurring question answered for the table: all three decide, know and check, and wait for nothing

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Manager: Someone Whose Work Is the Team ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: At about ten people every question queues at one founder's desk, so her judgment becomes the bottleneck

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Manager: Someone Whose Work Is the Team ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: A manager is added whose work is the team itself, along with agreed decision rights

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Manager: Someone Whose Work Is the Team ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: What the manager makes possible: same-day answers for the team and freed attention for the founder

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Manager: Someone Whose Work Is the Team ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The cost: the decider no longer does the work, so deciding and knowing are in different heads for the first time

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Manager: Someone Whose Work Is the Team ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Recurring question answered for the manager step: the manager decides, the workers know and check, everyone waits for the manager's time

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Product Manager: Someone Who Speaks for the Customer ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: At about twenty people conflicting requests pile up and nobody has time to judge which are worth building, so the loudest wins

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Product Manager: Someone Who Speaks for the Customer ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: A product manager is added to know the customers and decide what is built, while engineers decide how

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Product Manager: Someone Who Speaks for the Customer ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: What the product manager makes possible: customers are heard and builders get one ordered list they can finish

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Product Manager: Someone Who Speaks for the Customer ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The cost is a hand-off in which the reason gets lost, leaving a team judged on shipped features rather than customer outcomes (the feature factory)

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Product Manager: Someone Who Speaks for the Customer ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Recurring question answered for the product-manager step: what and how are decided by different people, nobody checks the customer outcome, and they wait for each other

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Split into Teams: More Than One Conversation ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: At about thirty people the number of possible conversations outgrows anyone's attention

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Split into Teams: More Than One Conversation ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The group is split into teams that each own a part sized to what they can hold in mind, their cognitive load

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Split into Teams: More Than One Conversation ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: What the split makes possible: each team is a small table again and the company grows by adding teams

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Split into Teams: More Than One Conversation ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The cost is the boundary between teams: without an agreed interface each team duplicates shared rules and the product mirrors the team structure (Conway)

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Split into Teams: More Than One Conversation ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Recurring question answered for the team split: each team decides, knows and checks its own part, nobody covers what crosses the line, and they wait for another team

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Platform Team: Build It Once for Everyone ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: With a dozen teams the same release, monitoring and storage work is done a dozen times, wasting attention and leaving faults unfixed elsewhere

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Platform Team: Build It Once for Everyone ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: A platform team is added to build the shared things once, ideally offered as self-service

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Platform Team: Build It Once for Everyone ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: What the platform team makes possible: product teams regain attention and the company has one way to release and one place to fix faults

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Platform Team: Build It Once for Everyone ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The cost is a team everyone depends on, whose request-based help makes every launch queue / A platform team can also build for a year something its nearby customers never wanted because it did not ask them

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Platform Team: Build It Once for Everyone ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Recurring question answered for the platform step: the platform team decides the tools and checks launches, product teams know their needs, and they wait in its queue

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Managers of Managers: Decisions Climb ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: With fifteen to twenty teams the queue reappears one level up, at the desk of the person all the managers report to

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Managers of Managers: Decisions Climb ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Teams are grouped under managers of managers, which introduces span and layer, with Larson's rule of thumb for sizes

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Managers of Managers: Decisions Climb ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: What the extra layer makes possible: every manager has someone with time for them and the top can hold a few groups in mind

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Managers of Managers: Decisions Climb ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The cost is distance: cross-group questions travel up and down and are decided from summaries / Once the organization is a chart, redrawing it becomes the default fix whether or not structure was the problem

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Managers of Managers: Decisions Climb ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Recurring question answered for the layers step: the common superior decides from a summary, the bottom knows, managers check by report, and all wait for the round trip

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Plan: Agreeing Once a Quarter ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: With several groups, competing top priorities cannot be settled below the top or case by case at the top, so cross-group judgment runs out

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Plan: Agreeing Once a Quarter ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Priorities and their people and money are written down and fixed for a period: the plan and its planning routine

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Plan: Agreeing Once a Quarter ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: What the plan makes possible: teams can rely on promised help and leaders can tell outsiders what is coming and its cost

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Plan: Agreeing Once a Quarter ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The cost is time: the plan is frozen at what was known when written, and the planning round is slow and can be blocked by one group

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Plan: Agreeing Once a Quarter ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Recurring question answered for the plan step: the quarterly round decides from old knowledge, teams know what changed, progress is checked against the plan, and all wait for the next round

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Ladder and the Metric: Judging Work You Cannot See ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: At several hundred people those who judge pay, promotion and funding cannot see the work, so verification from a distance runs out

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Ladder and the Metric: Judging Work You Cannot See ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Two substitutes for watching are added: a career ladder for people and metrics for teams, such as the DORA set

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Ladder and the Metric: Judging Work You Cannot See ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: What ladder and metric make possible: people are judged by one known standard and leaders can see team trends from afar

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Ladder and the Metric: Judging Work You Cannot See ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The cost is that people and teams serve the description and the number instead of the work, and visible rescues beat quiet prevention

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Ladder and the Metric: Judging Work You Cannot See ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Recurring question answered for the ladder and metric step: a committee decides from a case and a dashboard, those near the work know, the number checks only what it counts, and people wait for the promotion round

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Today: Every Structure at Once, and Software That Writes ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: No structure was removed when the next arrived, because each still helps someone, is someone's job, and nobody owns its removal

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Today: Every Structure at Once, and Software That Writes ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The present adds software that writes: coding agents draft changes in minutes while judging them takes as long as ever

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Today: Every Structure at Once, and Software That Writes ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The fictional company Corvane shows every structure in place plus coding agents, with merged changes up 2.4 times and review waits up from 5 to 31 hours

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Today: Every Structure at Once, and Software That Writes ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Recurring question answered for today: everyone decides a part, every earlier wait applies, and above all people wait for a human to check machine-written changes

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What the Steps Add Up To ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Introduces a table setting the nine steps side by side, with the failure names the next page will explain

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What the Steps Add Up To ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Tally: eight structures and eight waits now stand behind the one-day request, and each step pulled deciding, knowing and checking further apart

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What the Steps Add Up To ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The stack is not mere bureaucracy, since each structure answers a limit that returns if it is removed; but limits move, so ask what a structure was added for and whether the need still exists

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What the Steps Add Up To ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Hand-off: the next page names twelve failure patterns, each the price of one of these additions and tied to something a leader can design

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

results.draft_locus: The Ladder and the Metric: Judging Work You Cannot See ¶1 (boundary from The Plan ¶5)
results.quote: At several hundred people, those who decide on pay, promotion and funding have never seen most of the work they judge.
results.finding: The spec declares cause_effect carrying over 'several layers and a plan between the top and the work' as the reason the top can no longer see the work. The opening gives only headcount; neither the layers nor the plan is carried over, so the step follows the plan by size alone and not as its effect. Flow reader B independently noted: 'Why after the plan: unclear, only size.'
results.waived_by: Author (Željko Obrenović), 2026-11-19, rule 'max two rounds per chapter': the unit was revised after round 2 to address this finding and was not re-checked by fresh readers.

results.draft_locus: What the Steps Add Up To ¶1 (table, row 'Managers of managers'); Managers of Managers: Decisions Climb ¶4
results.quote: **The Escalation Ladder**, **The Org Chart as Architecture**, **The Reorg as Strategy**
results.finding: Flow reader A item 6 (a): 'The reorg and the escalation match that section's prose; this name seemed to match the Conway point in The Split into Teams, so I went back.' The layers step plants escalation and the reorg but never says what the spec's transition introduces ('a chart that can be mistaken for the organization'), so the name has no sentence in its own step to attach to and reads as belonging to the split step.
results.corroborated_by: Flow reader B item 3 (a): 'The only passage it seemed to match is Conway's point in the split-into-teams section, so I was unsure why it sits in this row.'
results.waived_by: Author (Željko Obrenović), 2026-11-19, rule 'max two rounds per chapter': the unit was revised after round 2 to address this finding and was not re-checked by fresh readers.

results.draft_locus: What the Steps Add Up To ¶2 (and ¶3, 'A review step sized for changes written by hand')
results.quote: Today adds an eighth wait, for a colleague to review a change.
results.finding: Flow reader B item 2 (a): 'Review was already present ... I went back to check whether this wait is new or only longer.' Review by a colleague is the final and largest wait and the conclusion's example of a structure to change, but it is not one of the eight structures and was introduced only in a subordinate clause of the split step's closing answer; the conclusion calls the wait 'added' today without saying that review existed since the split and only its length is new.
results.corroborated_by: Flow reader A item 5 (a), on the next paragraph's 'A review step sized for changes written by hand is an example.': 'Review is the final and largest wait, but it is not one of the eight structures ... I went back to find where review was introduced.' Same problem: where review entered and what status it has.
results.waived_by: Author (Željko Obrenović), 2026-11-19, rule 'max two rounds per chapter': the unit was revised after round 2 to address this finding and was not re-checked by fresh readers.

results.draft_locus: What the Steps Add Up To ¶2
results.quote: There are eight structures, and they brought seven waits
results.finding: Minor. Both flow readers stopped to count, each rating it (b): A item 4 'the ladder and the metric are two structures sharing one wait. The page does not say so'; B item 1 'I stopped to count'. The mismatch of eight and seven is left unexplained.
results.waived_by: Author (Željko Obrenović), 2026-11-19, rule 'max two rounds per chapter': the unit was revised after round 2 to address this finding and was not re-checked by fresh readers.

results.draft_locus: Three People at One Table: Nothing to Wait For ¶4 (promise), against the openings of The Manager, The Platform Team and Managers of Managers
results.quote: **Each step that follows begins where growth breaks one of these conditions**
results.finding: Minor, one reader at (a, mild). Flow reader B item 4: 'The manager, platform and managers-of-managers steps do not [say what has run out] ... I was left guessing which condition broke in those three.' The promise is made in terms of three conditions, but no later step names the condition it breaks, and three steps do not use the 'What has run out is ...' sentence either. Reader A item 1 (b) reports a related difficulty mapping conditions, capacities and the running question onto each other; not the same point, so not corroborated.
results.waived_by: Author (Željko Obrenović), 2026-11-19, rule 'max two rounds per chapter': the unit was revised after round 2 to address this finding and was not re-checked by fresh readers.

results.spec_locus: (outside the spec's units: Sources and Evidence)
results.quote: The table of steps in the text is in the order of the ideas, and its steps carry no dates, because they are common practice and not events.
results.finding: Minor. Both flow readers rated it (b): A item 7 'It nearly repeats the paragraph before it, and I briefly wondered which table was meant'; B item 5 'I re-read thinking I had lost my place'. The second paragraph of Sources repeats the first ('the year a source put an idea in writing') and refers to 'the table of steps' ambiguously, directly above a different table.
